title: June Solstice
direction: Watch the sunrise — it reaches its northernmost point on the horizon
description: The Sun reaches its northernmost point in the sky. The longest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere, and the shortest in the Southern. Many ancient sites like Stonehenge were aligned for this exact moment.
tips: Sunrise and sunset are at their most extreme positions on the horizon today.

title: Southern Delta Aquariids Meteor Shower
direction: Look south toward Aquarius after midnight
description: A reliable midsummer shower with long, slow glowing streaks. Overlaps with the early Perseids, making late July a rich week for meteor watching.
tips: Best after midnight under dark skies. Pair with early Perseids for a great night.

title: Alpha Capricornids Meteor Shower
description: Not huge in number, but famous for producing slow, dramatic fireball meteors that leave long glowing trails. A great companion shower to the Delta Aquariids.
tips: Watch from dark skies for the brightest fireballs.

title: Saturn at Opposition
direction: Rises in the east at sunset, highest around midnight
description: Saturn lines up directly opposite the Sun from Earth, making it brighter and bigger than at any other point of 2026. Even a small telescope will show the rings clearly.
tips: Even binoculars help. A telescope gives the best wow factor — the rings are unmistakable.

title: Total Solar Eclipse
visibility: Path of totality: Greenland, Iceland, Spain. Partial elsewhere in Europe, N. Africa, W. Asia
direction: Look toward the Sun — ONLY with certified eclipse glasses
description: The Moon completely covers the Sun for observers in the narrow path of totality. Outside the path, a partial eclipse is visible across a wide region. One of the most dramatic natural events possible.
tips: Never observe without certified solar eclipse glasses. If you're in the totality path, the few minutes of totality are safe to watch with naked eyes.
duration: Totality lasts a few minutes; partial phases ~2 hours

title: Perseid Meteor Shower
description: One of the best annual meteor showers. Debris from Comet Swift-Tuttle lights up the sky. Dark skies away from city lights give the best view — no telescope needed.
tips: Let your eyes adjust for 20 minutes. Lie flat on your back and look up.

title: Partial Lunar Eclipse
description: Earth's shadow partially covers the Moon, creating a dramatic dark bite out of its edge. The Moon may take on a reddish or darkened tint at the edge of the shadow.
tips: Safe to observe with naked eyes or binoculars. No special equipment needed.

title: Neptune at Opposition
direction: Look in Pisces constellation, low in the east after sunset
description: Neptune reaches its closest point to Earth for 2026. At magnitude 7.8 it's invisible to the naked eye, but binoculars reveal a blue-green 'star' that doesn't twinkle. A telescope shows its characteristic blue disk.
tips: Use binoculars or a telescope. Neptune looks like a tiny pale blue dot.

title: September Equinox
direction: Observe sunrise due east / sunset due west today
description: Day and night become approximately equal in length worldwide. In the Northern Hemisphere this marks the start of autumn; in the Southern, the start of spring.
tips: A great day to observe how precisely the Sun rises due east — ancient monuments were often aligned to this.

title: Draconid Meteor Shower
description: Usually modest, but Draconids occasionally produce dramatic outbursts with hundreds of meteors per hour when Earth passes through a dense debris clump. Worth keeping an eye on.
tips: One of the rare showers best watched in the evening rather than after midnight.

title: Orionid Meteor Shower
direction: Look toward Orion's raised arm (northeast) after midnight
description: Fast meteors shed by Halley's Comet, some of the fastest of any shower. They often leave persistent glowing trails. Orion rises around midnight so the best views are after 1 AM.
tips: Halley's debris hits at 66 km/s — expect brilliant streaks with long trails.

title: Jupiter at Opposition
direction: Rises in the east at sunset, highest around midnight in Taurus
description: Jupiter at its brightest and biggest of 2026. At magnitude -2.9 it outshines everything except Venus and the Moon. Even binoculars show the four Galilean moons. A small telescope reveals the cloud bands and the Great Red Spot.
tips: The four Galilean moons shift positions night to night — fascinating to track across a week.

title: Leonid Meteor Shower
direction: Look toward Leo constellation in the east
description: Famous for producing historic meteor storms every 33 years. In regular years it's a reliable mid-autumn show with fast, bright meteors from comet Tempel-Tuttle.
tips: Best after midnight when Leo is well above the horizon.

title: Geminid Meteor Shower
direction: Radiant near Castor in Gemini — look northeast from 9 PM onward
description: The king of annual meteor showers. Unusually, they come from an asteroid (3200 Phaethon) rather than a comet, producing multi-colored meteors — white, yellow, green, and red. Gemini rises early so you can start watching at 9 PM.
tips: This is the one not to miss. Bundle up — December is cold but skies are often clear.

title: Winter Solstice
direction: Watch the sunset — it sets at its most southwesterly point today
description: The shortest day in the Northern Hemisphere and the start of astronomical winter. The Sun reaches its lowest arc across the sky. After today, days slowly start growing longer again.
tips: A great night for stargazing — 16+ hours of darkness at northern latitudes.

title: Ursid Meteor Shower
direction: Look toward Ursa Minor (Little Dipper) in the north
description: A modest Christmas-season shower from debris of comet 8P/Tuttle. Circumpolar from northern latitudes — the radiant never sets, so you can watch all night.
tips: Low rates but a lovely backdrop for a cold December night.

title: Quadrantid Meteor Shower
direction: Look north toward the Boötes / Draco border
description: The first major shower of the year and potentially the strongest. Its peak lasts only a few hours, so timing is everything. Originates from asteroid 2003 EH1, thought to be an extinct comet.
tips: The peak is very short — check your local time carefully and be outside 30 minutes early.

title: Lyrid Meteor Shower
direction: Look toward Lyra constellation near bright star Vega
description: One of the oldest recorded meteor showers, observed for over 2,700 years. Debris from comet Thatcher. Occasional outbursts can push rates to 100/hr.
tips: Active before dawn. Vega rises around midnight — watch from 1 AM onward.

title: Eta Aquarid Meteor Shower
direction: Look east toward Aquarius before dawn
description: Halley's Comet meteors, entering from the north. Best from the Southern Hemisphere where rates hit 50/hr. From northern latitudes it's more modest, but the meteors that do appear are fast with long glowing tails.
tips: Best in the 2 hours before dawn.
